text: Everything so far happened in Power BI Desktop, the right tool for building. But the Merchandising Manager doesn't have Desktop open, and shouldn't need it. The Power BI Service is where a finished report actually gets handed to a stakeholder.

Publishing is Home ribbon, Publish, then choosing a destination workspace -- a shared workspace for Thornbury's BI team, not My Workspace, since My Workspace can't be shared with anyone else. Power BI uploads the report and the dataset as two related but separate objects, and a confirmation link appears once it finishes -- click it to open the report directly in the browser.

Even though they came from one file, the Service lists them separately. The dataset holds the model -- the table and the three measures -- and can be refreshed on a schedule. The report holds the pages and visuals a viewer actually sees. If this data needs refreshing next quarter, it's the dataset's refresh settings that matter, not the report's.

For sharing, this is one named stakeholder with no existing company-wide dashboard, so direct sharing is the right scope -- open the report in the Service, click Share, and enter the Merchandising Manager's work email, confirming they have at least Viewer access. A full Power BI App would be over-engineering here; that structure earns its place once multiple reports and multiple audiences exist.
With the report published and shared, it's ready to open on a laptop in the actual pricing review.
Next lesson is the two minutes this whole project was really built to support: presenting the dashboard back to the Merchandising Manager.
